name: Ahikam
title: Protector of the prophet Jeremiah
summary: Ahikam, son of the scribe Shaphan, was an influential official at the court in Judah toward the end of the kingdom. When the book of the law was rediscovered in the temple during King Josiah's reign, Ahikam was among those the king sent to the prophetess Huldah to seek the Lord's guidance. His most decisive action came when the prophet Jeremiah was threatened with death after his speech in the temple – Ahikam intervened and prevented Jeremiah from being killed. This act testifies to both personal courage and a deep respect for the prophetic word. Ahikam belonged to a family that played a key role in Judah's final decade: his son Gedaliah, after Jerusalem fell, was appointed by Nebuchadnezzar as governor over those remaining in the land, confirming the family's lasting influence.

keyEvents.title: The Book of the Law rediscovered in the temple
keyEvents.description: During the restoration of the temple in King Josiah's reign, the high priest Hilkiah found the Book of the Law. Shaphan, Ahikam's father and the king's scribe, brought the book to the king and read it to him. This discovery triggered a profound religious reformation in Judah.

keyEvents.title: The Delegation to the Prophetess Huldah
keyEvents.description: King Josiah sent a delegation that included Ahikam to consult the prophetess Huldah after the Book of the Law was found. Huldah's prophecy confirmed that God's judgment would fall on Judah, but that Josiah himself would be spared because of his humility.

keyEvents.title: Protection of Jeremiah After the Temple Sermon
keyEvents.description: After Jeremiah delivered his prophetic sermon in the temple and proclaimed Jerusalem's coming destruction, he was accused and threatened with death by priests, prophets, and the people. Ahikam used his influence to protect Jeremiah and prevented him from being handed over to the mob.

keyEvents.title: Gedaliah Appointed as Governor
keyEvents.description: After the fall of Jerusalem, Nebuchadnezzar appointed Gedaliah, son of Ahikam, as governor over those remaining in Judah. This appointment testifies to the prominent position of Ahikam's family and their political alignment with Jeremiah's message.

versions.summary: Ahikam was the son of Shaphan the scribe and a prominent official at the court of Judah. He is best known for protecting the prophet Jeremiah from those who sought to kill him. His son Gedaliah was later appointed governor over Judah after Babylon's conquest of Jerusalem.

versions.reason: [minor] Ahikam was more than just a 'leader'. He was a court official/advisor and specifically known as the protector of Jeremiah. The roles should be expanded to better reflect this.; [minor] The events 'Protection of Jeremiah' and 'Jeremiah's Temple Sermon and Trial' overlap significantly – both concern the same episode in Jeremiah 26. These should be merged into one event to avoid duplication.; [minor] Shaphan also had a son named Jaazaniah (Ezekiel 8:11), who is sometimes mentioned as a brother. It may be worth considering including him, but it is uncertain whether all the named sons of Shaphan are from the same Shaphan. Elasa and Gemariah are well documented as sons of Shaphan the scribe.; [major] The profile lacks footnotes. Notes on historical, linguistic, and archaeological details related to Ahikam and the family of Shaphan should be added.

versions.summary: Ahikam was the son of Shaphan the scribe and a prominent official at the court of Judah. He was part of the delegation King Josiah sent to the prophetess Huldah after the Book of the Law was rediscovered in the temple. He is best known for protecting the prophet Jeremiah from those who sought to kill him after the temple sermon. Ahikam belonged to an influential family that played a key role in Judah's final decade; his son Gedaliah was later appointed governor over Judah after Babylon's conquest of Jerusalem.

versions.reason: [minor] The title 'Shaphan Finds the Book of the Law' is somewhat imprecise. It was actually the high priest Hilkiah who found the book, and Shaphan brought it to the king. The title should reflect this more accurately.; [major] The description states that 'Ahikam's father Shaphan was the scribe who brought the rediscovered Book of the Law to King Josiah,' but it was the high priest Hilkiah who found the book. Shaphan read it to the king. Ahikam is not directly involved in this event—it concerns more the background of the delegation sent to Huldah.; [minor] Shaphan had several well-known sons. In addition to Elasa (Jer 29:3) and Gemariah (Jer 36:10), some scholars also mention Jaazaniah (Ezek 8:11), although his connection to the family of Shaphan is debated. It may be worth considering including him, but the current list is acceptable based on the most secure references.; [minor] The summary is good, but it could be improved with a bit more theological depth regarding the significance of Ahikam's actions in light of God's protection of His prophets, and varied somewhat from the previous version.

footnotes.text: The name Ahikam (אֲחִיקָם) means 'my brother has risen' or 'my brother has stood up' in Hebrew, composed of אָח (akh, 'brother') and קוּם (qum, 'to rise'). Such family-based names were common in ancient Israel and could express gratitude, hope, or a confession tied to family relationships.

The Shaphan family was one of the most influential official families in late Judah. Shaphan served as scribe under King Josiah, and several of his sons and grandsons—Ahikam, Elasa, Gemariah, and Gedaliah—held prominent positions. The family appears consistently sympathetic to Jeremiah's prophetic message.

In the Lachish Letters (ostraca found at Tel Lachish from about 588–586 BC), several officials from this period are mentioned. Although Ahikam is not directly named, these letters provide valuable insight into the political climate and communication structure in Judah just before Jerusalem's fall.

Ahikam's protection of Jeremiah (Jer 26:24) illustrates a recurring biblical pattern where God uses influential individuals to preserve the lives and messages of prophets. A similar act is seen with Obadiah, who hid one hundred prophets from Jezebel (1 Kgs 18:3–4).

The fact that Gedaliah, son of Ahikam, was appointed by Nebuchadnezzar as governor over Judah after Jerusalem's fall (2 Kgs 25:22) suggests the family held a known pro-Babylonian stance. This political alignment coincided with Jeremiah's message to submit to Babylon as an expression of God's will.

A bulla impression (seal mark) bearing the inscription 'Gedalyahu who is over the house' was found at Lachish. Many scholars identify this with Ahikam's son Gedaliah, which would provide a direct archaeological link to Ahikam's family.
